title: Ezekiel 44:1–3
context: The vision continues, and Ezekiel, the prophet, narrates. His guide brings him back to the outer east gate of the sanctuary, and it is shut. The LORD tells Ezekiel that the gate must stay shut and no one may enter by it, because the LORD, the God of Israel, has entered by it, recalling the glory’s return through the east gate in 43:1–5, the reverse of its departure in 10:18–19 and 11:23. Only the prince may sit in the gate to eat bread before the LORD, entering and leaving by the porch. The prince appears often in chapters 44–48. Ezekiel elsewhere calls the coming David a prince (34:24; 37:25), but the prince here also offers a sin offering for himself (45:22) and has sons and an inheritance (46:16), so interpreters differ on whether he is a messianic figure, an ordinary ruler of the restored community, or a figure that points ahead in some partial way. The identification is best held with care, with the promise to David (2 Samuel 7:13, 16) kept in view. Readers in both traditions take the temple vision of chapters 40–48 in the ways named at 40:1–16: as a plan for a literal future temple, as a symbolic or ideal picture of God dwelling with his people, or as fulfilled in Christ and the church. Arminian and Reformed readers generally treat the holiness of the LORD’s presence as shared ground.

verses.text: Then he brought me back by the way of the outer gate of the sanctuary, which looks toward the east; and it was shut.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Ezekiel brought back to the outer east gate and finding it shut. The vision continues to reveal how God orders his dwelling.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the shut gate as a sign that the LORD’s presence has returned (compare 43:1–5). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse within the larger temple vision.

verses.text: The LORD said to me, “This gate shall be shut. It shall not be opened, no man shall enter in by it; for the LORD, the God of Israel, has entered in by it. Therefore it shall be shut.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD telling Ezekiel the gate must stay shut because the LORD has entered by it. The place of his entry is set apart.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the holiness of God’s presence honored by the closed gate. Both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about reverence for the LORD who dwells among his people.

verses.text: As for the prince, he shall sit in it as prince to eat bread before the LORD. He shall enter by the way of the porch of the gate, and shall go out the same way.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the prince sitting in the gate to eat before the LORD, entering and leaving by the porch. He has a place of honor but under God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a privileged but limited role for the prince. Readers in both traditions commonly hold the prince’s identity with care, keeping the promise to David in view (compare 34:24).
